To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
older adults have difficulty with belief-desire reasoning when executive demands are high, but not when executive demands are low.

(1) belief-desire reasoning is impaired in older adults relative to younger adults, (2) this impairment can be attributed to executive control deficits, rather than to a deficit in the representation of mental states, (3) this impairment is not specific to belief-desire reasoning, but rather extends to other types of reasoning, and (4) this impairment can, in part, be ameliorated by training on executive control tasks.

1) older adults are as capable as younger adults at reasoning about beliefs and desires when executive demands are low; 2) when executive demands are high, older adults are disproportionately affected by the demands, and this effect is due to age-related decline in processing speed and inhibition.

older adults have the same capacity as younger adults to reason about mental states.

the executive selection system is a critical component of the belief-desire system and its breakdown may be a major factor in the decline of social cognition with age.
